description: We are Team Charlie's Angels, a group of enthusiastic learners and doers who turn ideas into working solutions. We bring skills in full-stack development, data processing, AI, and UI/UX design, and we thrive on learning fast and delivering under pressure. We joined the NASA Space Apps Challenge to show what we’re capable of and to put our skills to use for a meaningful, impactful cause. We believe technology should be powerful, accessible, and built to make a real difference.
summary: COMPASS is a route planner for the first people to walk on Mars. Today's Mars map viewers show data but do not plan a walk. COMPASS joins orbital and rover data from several NASA missions into one screen for Jezero Crater. It rates every 60 m cell of the map with an estimated safety and a sampling-likeness score, then finds three genuinely different routes (Safest, Best science, Fastest). Each route comes with the best start time inside the crew's window, a supplies check with a 25% reserve, and a point of no return, the last place from which the crew can still walk home. Every number opens into its parts, so a crew can see why a route ranks where it does. It matters because help from Earth is 4 to 24 minutes away, so a crew must decide on the spot. Mission teams can also upload their own data to retrain the estimators.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

COMPASS plans a Marswalk in Jezero Crater. The user sets a start, a destination, a time window, crew size and travel mode. COMPASS returns three ranked routes. Each shows depart, arrive and back times, whether supplies are enough, the point of no return, and an estimated safety from 0 to 100. A Walk view then tracks oxygen and the way home during the trip.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Gather: elevation, imagery, thermal images, the Perseverance traverse, weather and geology from NASA and USGS are cut to a 60 m grid of about 30 by 30 km (268,128 cells).

2. Estimate: two machine-learning estimators (scikit-learn) rate every cell. A safety estimator (random forest) and a sampling-likeness estimator (gradient boosting, trained on 24 real sample sites) are tested on unseen map blocks (AUC 0.976 and 0.945). A hard 25 degree slope limit overrides them.

3. Plan: A* search finds three different routes. Each is scored 0.6 x terrain + 0.2 x daylight and temperature + 0.2 x supplies margin. The sun position is computed for the sol, and a 25% supply reserve is required.

4. Explain: every score opens into its formula and inputs. Users can upload traverse logs, sample results, weather or surface-change files to retrain the estimators.

HONEST LIMITS

Safety labels are mostly rule-based, and only 0.4% come from real traverse cells. There are no real unsafe labels, because a rover drives only where it thinks it is safe. Plain slope matches the rover's measured tilt slightly better than our model. For these reasons the output is called an estimated safety, not a safety rating. It covers Jezero Crater only, and weather is the last published rover data.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

It turns data NASA already holds into a decision a crew can make locally, in minutes, with the way home always shown. Roadmap: analog field tests (Mars Desert Research Station, HI-SEAS), then the Moon, then a Mars crew companion that runs offline.

TOOLS

React, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet, Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn, NumPy, pandas, Docker, Render, GitHub.

CREATIVITY

The product is a single planner that combines safety, time, supplies and science. Features include the point of no return, the best start time, "Explain" on every score, and estimators that retrain on uploaded mission data. We chose to be open about validity and limits.
